parole.significato: forms female given names, usually from male given names, e.g. Gíslína from Gísli, Sæmundína from Sæmundur, but sometime…
parole.testo: From Latin -īna and its derived forms in other European languages, such as Danish -ine, present in many borrowed names and subsequently used independently to form new Icelandic names.

From Latin amalgama, from Medieval Latin amalgama (“mercury alloy”), from Arabic اَلْمَلْغَم (al-malḡam, “emollient poultice or unguent for sores”), from Ancient Greek μάλαγμα (málagma, “emollient; malleable material”), from μαλάσσω (malássō, “to soften”), from μαλακός (malakós, “soft”).

parole.significato: at the end of prayers: so be it

parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin antilops, from Byzantine Greek ἀνθόλοψ (anthólops).
Borrowed from Latin atomus (“smallest particle”), from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos, “indivisible”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).

parole.significato: Advent (season of the church year leading up to Christmas)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin barbarus (“foreigner, barbarian, uncivilized person”).

Borrowed from Latin biblia (“collection of books”), from Ancient Greek βιβλία (biblía, “books”), plural of βιβλίον (biblíon, “book”), originally a diminutive of βίβλος (bíblos), from βύβλος (búblos, “papyrus”) (from the ancient Phoenician city of Byblos which exported this writing material).
Learned borrowing from Latin dēbet (“he/she/it owes”), from dēbeō.
Borrowed from Latin differō, from dis- (“apart”) + ferō (“carry, bear”).

parole.significato: to nap, to sleep, to rest, to be idle
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dormīre, from Proto-Italic *dormiō, from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥m-yé-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”) + *-yéti.

From the 18th century; probably derived from the Latin dōdrāns (“three quarters”), from dē quadrāns (“from one quarter”). "Three quarters" most likely originally referred to the format or size of the book.
From Latin dominātus, perfect active participle of dominor (“rule, have dominion”), from dominus (“lord, master”); see dominus.
From Latin firmō, probably via Middle Low German.

parole.significato: peach (fruit of the tree Prunus persica)

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin fauna, from Latin Fauna (“name of a rural goddess”).
Ultimately from Latin fīnis; see English fine.
Borrowed from Late Latin vocatus, from Classical Latin advocatus, compare German Vogt.

parole.significato: gradual (service book for the mass) (refers primarily to the Graduale of Guðbrandur Þorláksson since its publication in…

parole.testo: From Latin hyaena, from Ancient Greek ὕαινα (húaina).
Euphemistic form of Jesús minn eini (“Jesus, my one and only”), which may itself be a folk-etymological alteration of Latin Jesu domine (“Lord Jesus”). Compare for this German jemine.
Uncertain, but probably either from Jesús og María (“Jesus and Mary”), or alternatively from Latin Jesu domine (“Lord Jesus”), which is also a likely origin of the form je minn eini (see there).
Learned borrowing from New Latin Iēsūīta.
From Latin calx, probably via Middle Low German.
From Latin calamus (“sweet flag; calamus”) + rót (“root”).
Ultimately from Late Latin capulum, probably through Danish kabel.
From kapp (“eagerness, zeal”), ultimately from Latin campus.
Borrowed from Latin catholicus, from Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós, “universal”), from κατά (katá, “according to”) + ὅλος (hólos, “whole”).
Borrowed from Latin, from Ancient Greek χερούβ (kheroúb), from Hebrew.

From Vulgar Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from Ancient Greek κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), ultimately possibly of Anatolian origin.

parole.significato: cellar, basement (lowest floor of a house)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Late Latin cellārium, through late Old Norse kellari (and Middle Low German keller). Compare Faroese kjallari, Swedish källare, Norwegian kjeller.
Shortened from kommúnisti, derived from Latin commūnis (“common”).
Learned borrowing from Latin crocus, from Ancient Greek κρόκος (krókos).
Learned borrowing from New Latin chrōmium.
From Medieval Latin cursarius, ultimately from currō (“to run”). Compare French corsaire, English corsair.
Borrowed from Latin cholera, from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra), from χολή (kholḗ, “bile”).
Borrowed from Latin cōlon, from Ancient Greek κώλον (kṓlon).

parole.significato: hollow hemispherical object; bowl, dome, helmet

parole.testo: From Medieval Latin lagellum, diminutive of earlier Latin lagēna (“earthenware vessel; flask, flagon”). Cognate with Danish legel, Swedish lägel.

parole.significato: horde, multitude (a host of something uncountable)

parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin lēctiō (“reading”), from Latin legō (“gather, collect; read”), from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- (“to gather”).
Borrowed from Latin mārtiī, genitive singular of mārtius (“relating to Mars”), from Mārs (“Mars, Roman god of war and agriculture”).

parole.significato: mass (quantity of matter cohering together to make one body)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nānus (“dwarf”), from Ancient Greek νᾶνος (nânos).
From Latin nona hora (literally “the ninth hour”). See also the English word noon.

parole.significato: November (the eleventh month of the Gregorian calendar, following October and preceding December)

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pardus, from Ancient Greek πάρδος (párdos).

parole.significato: paten (plate for the host during Eucharist)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin patīna, from Ancient Greek πατάνη (patánē).

parole.significato: a sheet or card with the Latin phrase pax vobiscum (“peace be with you”) to kiss during the kiss of peace at mass

parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin pelicānus, variant of pelecānus, from Ancient Greek πελεκάς (pelekás).
Borrowed from the neuter of Latin pendulus (“hanging, pendent”).
Ultimately from Latin penicillum, probably via Danish pensel.
A loanword ultimately from Latin pedes (“footsoldier”).

parole.significato: plant (an organism of the kingdom Plantae, and now specifically, a living organism of the Embryophyta (land plants) or…
a pleb, a common person (person out of their class at an event or gathering)
parole.testo: Coined by Icelandic comedian and mayor of Reykjavík Jón Gnarr in 2002 (in his novel Plebbabókin, Literally, “The Book of Plebs”). The word is from Latin plēbs (“plebeians, common people”), the lower class in Ancient Rome.
Learned borrowing from Latin praedicō (“proclaim, declare, preach”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European roots *preh₂- and *deyḱ-.
From Latin per centum (“by one hundred”).

Borrowed from Late Latin protocollum (“the first sheet of a volume (on which contents and errata were written)”), from Byzantine Greek πρωτόκολλον (prōtókollon, “first sheet glued onto a manuscript”), from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”) + κόλλα (kólla, “glue”).
Verbal formation related to páll (“spade, pale”), itself from Latin pālus (“stake, prop”) via Old English pāl.
Borrowed from Latin polīticus, most likely via some Northern European language (cf. Dutch politicus).
Borrowed from Latin pulsus (“beat”), from pellere (“drive”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin pupa, from special use of Latin pūpa.
rót (“root”) + tækur (“acceptable”), apparently a calque of Latin rādīcālis (“having roots, radical”), as well as a partial cognate of the Latin.
From Medieval Latin rotulāre (“to roll; to revolve”), from Latin rotula (“a little wheel”), diminutive of rota (“a wheel”).

Borrowed from Latin satira, from earlier satura, from lanx satura (“full dish”), from feminine of satur. Altered in Latin by influence of Ancient Greek σάτυρος (sáturos, “satyr”), on the mistaken notion that the form is related to the Greek σατυρικόν δράμα (saturikón dráma, “satyr drama”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin secunda, short for secunda pars minuta (“second diminished part (of the hour)”).

parole.significato: September (the ninth month of the Gregorian calendar, following August and preceding October, containing the southward…

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).
From sléttur + söngur, calque of Latin cantus planus.
Learned borrowing from Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos).
Shortened from spíritus, from Latin spīritus.

From steinn (“stone”) + brjótur (“breaker”); a calque of Late Latin saxifraga, from earlier Latin saxifragus (“stone-breaking, stone-crushing”). Compare German Steinbrech, Danish stenbræk, Dutch steenbreek.

parole.significato: stemma (diagram showing the relationship of variants of a text)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin stemma (“garland, wreath; pedigree, family tree”), from Ancient Greek στέμμα (stémma, “garland, wreath”).

parole.significato: a sum; (a quantity obtained by addition or aggregation)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin summa (“sum, summary, total”).
Borrowed, through another European language, from Latin cithara.

parole.significato: a socle, a plinth beneath a statue or other artwork
tenor (musical range, person or instrument in that range)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tenor (literally “holder”), from teneō (“hold”).

parole.significato: to throw (a person) up into the air (done by a group for celebration or as an initiation rite)
parole.testo: Originated in the language of grammar school pupils, derived from Latin tollō (“lift up”).
A diminutive of Latin dēlīrium tremēns.
From Latin turris (“tower”). Cognate with Danish tårn and German Turm. First appears in the 12th or 13th century.
Literally, “(the) time flies”. Calque of Latin tempus fugit.
Calque of Latin circumcīdō, from um (“around”) + skera (“to cut”).

parole.significato: circumcised (having had either male or female circumcision)
parole.testo: From umskera (“circumcise”), calque of Latin circumcīdō, from skera um (literally “to cut around”).
Borrowed from Latin villa (“villa, estate, large country residence”).
From viðtenging (“annexation, connection”) + háttur (“mood”), a calque of Latin modus coniūnctīvus, since the subjunctive is frequently used when connecting a main clause with subordinate clauses.
Borrowed from Latin aura, from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra).

parole.significato: pip (one of the spots on a die)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ās, perhaps via Middle Low German [Term?].
From Late Latin adventūra (“adventure”), via Middle Low German êventü̂re.
Learned borrowing from Latin opium, from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion), from ὀπός (opós, “juice of a plant”), from Proto-Indo-European *swokʷos (“juice, resin”).

Borrowed from New Latin Ūtopia, the name of a fictional island possessing a seemingly perfect socio-politico-legal system in the book Utopia (1516) by Sir Thomas More. Coined from Ancient Greek οὐ (ou, “not”) + τόπος (tópos, “place, region”) + -ία (-ía).
